proposals.observation: In the last 48 hours, 4 sessions hit the quiz intro page. Zero started the quiz. The furthest_step_distribution shows all 4 stopped at intro_load — meaning the intro screen itself is the drop-off point. Three of those 4 sessions arrived direct, so these are warm visitors (bookmarks, returning traffic, or link-share from someone who already trusts Joel). They loaded the page, read something, and left without pressing start.
proposals.proposal: The intro screen is doing too much persuading and not enough orienting. Warm, returning visitors already have some buy-in — they don't need to be sold the quiz again on the intro screen. They need one clear, low-threat reason to press the button right now. The current CTA text almost certainly sounds like a commitment ("find out your money type") when these visitors are in a quiet, uncertain mood. Replace the intro copy with a single grounded line that names what the quiz actually does in concrete terms, then a button that sounds like a small first step rather than a declaration. Avoid any language that implies the result will fix something — the ICP is 25-35, earns well, already suspicious of promises.

proposals.impact: lift Money Worship open rate toward Vigilance benchmark
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 66.67% open rate across 12 sends. Money Worship sits at 37.5% across 16 sends — 29 percentage points lower, with more sends. The subject line or sender preview for the Worship sequence is almost certainly not doing the same work as Vigilance. Money Vigilance as a script naturally lends itself to honest, slightly uncomfortable subject lines ("you check your account more than you'd admit"). Money Worship subject lines probably skew aspirational or instructional, which is the register the ICP has learned to ignore.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line (and preview text if set) of the first email in the Money Worship automation. The goal is to match the register that makes Vigilance perform: specific, slightly uncomfortable, about a behaviour the reader recognises in themselves rather than a result they want. The Worship script's core insight is that the person ties self-worth to net worth — so the subject line should reflect a moment that feels true, not a promise.

proposals.impact: route high-intent blog readers into quiz funnel
proposals.observation: The blog post published today ("Why does sorting my finances feel impossible when everything else is already overwhelming?") targets exactly the avoidance-and-overload mindset of the ICP — someone who earns well, feels capable elsewhere, but keeps not starting with money. This is one of the highest-intent search and share queries in the set. The post has no data showing an internal link to the quiz, and the quiz sits at zero starts. A reader who finishes this post is primed: they've just read 600-900 words that describes their situation. The next logical step is the quiz, but only if it's offered in a way that doesn't feel like a funnel.
proposals.proposal: Add a single inline call-to-action near the end of the blog post body — after the main argument lands, before any closing remarks — that points to the quiz. The framing must not sound like a promotion. It should sound like a natural next thought: "if this post named something real for you, here is a four-minute set of questions that goes one layer further." No hype, no urgency, no promise of a result that changes everything.
proposals.new_text:
If this post named something you've been circling for a while, there's a short set of questions on this site that goes one layer further. It looks at the thinking pattern underneath the avoidance — not to label you, but because most people find it easier to act once they can see the thing clearly. It takes about four minutes.
